docs.title: (1) Core Idea of Evidence-Based Management
docs.text:
Evidence-Based Practice (EBP) is about making better-quality decisions:

Good decisions should be based on:

  • Critical thinking
  • The best available evidence

Most managers do use evidence in decision-making, but they often pay too little attention to the quality of that evidence

  • As a result, decisions are often based on:

    • unfounded beliefs
    • management fads
    • popular ideas promoted by management gurus

  • Relying on weak or low-quality evidence can lead to:

    • bad decisions
    • poor outcomes
    • limited understanding of why things go wrong

Evidence-Based Practice aims to improve the way decisions are made. It helps practitioners:

  • evaluate how much they can trust the evidence they already have
  • identify and search for additional relevant evidence
  • use evidence more systematically in everyday work

docs.title: (2) Definition & Steps of Evidence-Based Management
docs.text:
Evidence-based management is about making decisions through the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of the best available evidence from multiple sources.

Evidence-Based Management: Six-A Framework: Six steps to increase the likelihood of a favorable outcome:

  • Ask: Translate a practical issue or problem into an answerable question
  • Acquire: Systematically search for and retrieve evidence
  • Appraise: Critically judge the trustworthiness and relevance of the evidence
  • Aggregate: Weigh and pull together the evidence
  • Apply: Incorporate the evidence into to the decision-making process
  • Assess: Evaluate the outcome of the decision taken

Example of Applying the Six-A Framework: High Employee Turnover

Analysing high employee turnover in a company using the Six-A Framework:

  • Ask: What are the causes of high employee turnover in our company?

  • Acquire: Search for relevant data and information, e.g.,

    • exit interviews
    • employee surveys
    • industry benchmarks

  • Appraise: Evaluate the quality and relevance of the evidence, e.g.,

    • Are the exit interviews conducted systematically?
    • Are the employee surveys representative?
    • Are the industry benchmarks comparable?

  • Aggregate: Synthesize the evidence to identify common themes and patterns, e.g.,

    • Are there recurring reasons for leaving?
    • Are there specific departments or roles with higher turnover?
    • Are there any correlations between turnover and factors like compensation, work environment, or career development opportunities?

  • Apply: Develop and implement strategies to address the identified causes, e.g.,

    • Improve employee engagement
    • Enhance compensation and benefits
    • Provide career development opportunities

  • Assess: Monitor the impact of the implemented strategies on employee turnover rates, e.g.,

    • Track turnover rates over time
    • Conduct follow-up surveys
    • Gather feedback from employees to evaluate the effectiveness of the interventions

docs.title: (3) Definition of Evidence
docs.text:
In Evidence-Based Practice, evidence basically means information:

  • Evidence is not limited to numbers or statistics.

  • Evidence can be:

    • quantitative (numbers, metrics, statistics)
    • qualitative (descriptions, observations, experiences)

Evidence can come from different types of information, such as:

  1. Scientific research

    • Published studies and academic findings

    • Helps identify generally applicable facts about:

      • People
      • Organizations
      • Management practices

  2. Organizational or business data

    • Internal company information

    • For example:

      • Performance metrics
      • Financial indicators
      • Operational observations
      • Business conditions

  3. Professional experience

    • The experience and judgment of practitioners can also count as evidence
    • An entrepreneur’s previous experience building different businesses may provide useful insight into what is likely to work

Key Principle of Evidence-Based Practice:

  • Any type of evidence can be used

    • Management decisions should be based on different forms of evidence
    • Not just one source

  • But it should only be included if it is:

    • Trustworthy
    • Relevant

docs.title: (4) Reasons for Using Evidence-Based Management
docs.text:
Management based on experiences and judgment:

  • Most management decisions are not based on the best available evidence

  • Instead, many practitioners make decisions mainly based on:

    • personal experience
    • personal judgment

Three problems with this approach:

  1. Personal Judgment Alone Is Not Enough

    • Personal judgment is often not a reliable source of evidence, and experience alone does not automatically lead to good decisions

    • This is because people are vulnerable to:

      • systematic errors
      • cognitive biases
      • information-processing limitations

    • As a result:

      • Decision quality can be poor
      • Even experienced professionals can make weak forecasts or bad judgments

    • Examples of areas where human judgment can be weak:

      • credit ratings
      • economic forecasting
      • political developments
      • medical diagnoses

  2. Blindly Copying “Best Practices”

    • Practitioners often copy what other organizations are doing

    • This usually happens through:

      • benchmarking
      • so-called “best practices”

    • This is risky because:

      • A practice that works in one organization may not work in another

      • Different organizations have:

        • different contexts
        • different cultures
        • different goals
        • different constraints

    • Important point: Benchmarking can provide ideas, but it is not proof that something will work in your own situation

  3. Barriers to Evidence-Based Practice

    • Lack of training: Many practitioners have not been trained to:

      • evaluate evidence critically
      • judge trustworthiness and relevance

    • Poor access to organizational information: Important data may be:

      • hard to access
      • incomplete
      • low quality

    • Lack of awareness of scientific evidence

      • Many practitioners are not familiar with current research

      • This creates a gap between:

        • what managers believe works
        • what research actually shows works

Research on Evidence-Based Management

Survey findings:

  • A survey of 950 American HR practitioners found a large gap between:

    • what practitioners think is effective
    • what scientific research shows is effective

  • Similar findings were reported in other countries

Meaning of this finding

  • Many managers rely too much on:

    • personal experience
    • “best practices”
    • leadership beliefs

  • And too little on:

    • scientific evidence
    • organizational evidence

Consequences of not using evidence-based practice

  • Organizations may spend huge amounts of money on management practices that are:

    • ineffective
    • or even harmful

  • This can negatively affect:

    • organizations
    • employees
    • clients

Case Example: Importance of Evidence-Based Practice

Situation:

  • An American IT company believed for years that technical expertise was the most important quality of a good manager

  • The company assumed that the best managers were those who:

    • Let employees work independently
    • Only stepped in when technical problems occurred

  • The company found that when employees were asked what they valued most in a manager:

    • Technical expertise ranked last

    • Employees valued other qualities more, such as:

      • Asking good questions
      • Taking time to meet
      • Caring about employees’ careers and lives

This shows that managers with these people-oriented qualities had:

  • Top-performing teams
  • Happier employees
  • Lower staff turnover

Main Lesson from the Case

  • The company relied too long on an assumption
  • But scientific evidence had already shown that supportive, communicative managers are more effective
  • If the company had used evidence earlier, it could have improved management practices much sooner

docs.title: 2. Sources of Evidence in Management Decision-Making
docs.text:
Decision-makers should look for evidence from multiple sources:

  • Scientific evidence: Findings from published scientific research
  • Organizational evidence: Data, facts and figures gathered from the organization
  • Experiential evidence: The professional experience and judgment of practitioners
  • Stakeholder evidence: The values and concerns of people who may be affected by the decision

docs.title: (1) Scientific Evidence
docs.text:
Scientific evidence refers to findings from published scientific research, especially studies published in academic journals

  • Management research is growing rapidly.

  • There is also useful research from outside management, such as:

    • psychology
    • communication
    • decision science
    • organizational behavior

Scientific evidence is important because:

  • Scientific research provides evidence about:

    • what tends to work
    • what does not work
    • under what conditions something is effective

  • It is useful because many management problems are not unique.

  • Similar issues often appear across:

    • organizations
    • industries
    • countries
    • professional settings

To use scientific evidence well, practitioners need to:

  • know how to search for relevant studies

  • be able to judge:

    • trustworthiness
    • relevance
    • applicability to their own context

Case Example – Scientific Evidence

Situation:

  • A large Canadian law firm planned to merge with a smaller nearby firm.

  • The goal was to integrate only the back office:

    • IT
    • Finance
    • Facilities

  • The legal practices and front office would remain separate.

  • Partners believed that cultural differences between the two firms might create serious problems.

What Scientific Evidence Showed:

  • A meta-analysis of 46 studies with a combined sample of 10,710 mergers and acquisitions was found.

  • The study showed:

    • Cultural differences can hurt merger effectiveness
    • But mainly when the intended level of integration is high

Key Insight: In mergers with low integration, cultural differences may actually be associated with benefits.

docs.title: (2) Organizational Evidence
docs.text:
Organizational evidence refers to data, facts, and figures gathered from the organization itself.

Possible Forms of Organizational Evidence

  • Hard data

    • Cash flow
    • Costs
    • Return on investment (ROI)
    • Market share
    • Customer satisfaction scores
    • Repeat business
    • Product return rates
    • Staff turnover
    • Productivity levels
    • Medical errors

  • Soft data

    • Employee perceptions
    • Attitudes toward senior management
    • Organizational culture
    • Job satisfaction

Organizational evidence is important because it is essential for:

  • identifying problems
  • understanding likely causes
  • evaluating possible solutions
  • deciding what is needed for implementation

Case Example – Organizational Evidence

Situation:

  • A large insurance company planned to change its structure - from regional to product-based

  • Management Assumption: The board believed restructuring would:

    • Improve market presence
    • Increase customer focus

  • Concern from Sales Managers: Sales managers argued that removing the regional structure would:

    • Weaken customer relationships
    • Reduce customer service quality

What Organizational Evidence Showed: Internal analysis found:

  • Customer satisfaction was already above industry average

  • There was a strong negative correlation between:

    • Account managers’ travel expenses
    • Customer satisfaction

Interpretation:

  • Sales managers who lived closer to customers had higher customer satisfaction
  • The board decided to keep the regional structure

docs.title: (3) Experiential Evidence
docs.text:
Experiential evidence refers to the professional experience and judgment of practitioners, which includes:

  • Managers
  • Consultants
  • Business leaders
  • Experienced professionals

Experiential evidence is not just intuition, opinion, or belief. It is based on "Tacit knowledge":

  • Repeated experience
  • Reflection on outcomes
  • Lessons learned over time

Professional experience is important because it can help practitioners judge:

  • whether an issue really needs attention
  • whether internal data are trustworthy
  • whether research findings fit the situation
  • whether a proposed solution is likely to work in practice

Case Example – Experiential Evidence

Situation:

  • A university hospital asked nurses to prepare personal development plans

  • These plans focused on:

    • Aspirations
    • Career priorities

  • HR Director’s Argument:

    • The HR director used Maslow’s hierarchy of needs

    • He argued that nurses in the emergency department should be excluded because:

      • They were facing serious safety hazards
      • Basic needs should come before professional development

  • What Experienced Practitioners Said:

    • Experienced managers and nurses disagreed
    • Their professional experience suggested that nurses in difficult environments are often more interested in development and self-improvement

Additional Evidence:

  • Scientific database searches found:
  • No strong empirical support for Maslow’s theory in this context

Conclusion:

  • The nurses’ view was accepted
  • The program was not restricted in the way the HR director proposed

docs.title: (4) Stakeholder Evidence
docs.text:
Stakeholder evidence refers to the values and concerns of people who may be affected by a decision.

Stakeholders includes:

  • Internal stakeholders

    • Employees
    • Managers
    • Board members

  • External stakeholders

    • Suppliers
    • Customers
    • Shareholders
    • Government
    • The public

Stakeholder evidence is important because it helps decision-makers understand:

  • What different groups consider important
  • How people are likely to react to decisions
  • Whether a decision is likely to be accepted or resisted

Examples of Stakeholder Priorities: Different stakeholders may care more about:

  • Short-term gain vs long-term sustainability
  • Employee well-being vs employee output
  • Organizational reputation vs profitability
  • Participation vs top-down control

Case Example – Stakeholder Evidence

Situation:

  • A telecommunications company conducted a survey on employee satisfaction with supervisors

    • The survey was sent to 12,500 employees

    • It included demographic questions such as:

      • postcode
      • date of birth
      • job title

  • Problem:

    • Only 582 employees responded
    • Response rate was less than 5%

What Stakeholder Evidence Showed:

  • A focus group was held with employees

  • Employees explained that they were worried demographic data could:

    • reveal their identity
    • make the survey not truly anonymous

What Was Changed: The company:

  • removed postcode
  • replaced date of birth with an age range

Result & Conclusion:

  • The revised survey achieved a 67% response rate

  • Understanding stakeholder concerns helped improve:

    • Participation
    • Trust
    • The usefulness of the data collected

docs.title: (1) Critically Appraising Evidence
docs.text:
Critical appraisal means assessing whether evidence is:

  • Trustworthy
  • Relevant
  • Sufficient
  • Free from serious bias

Reasons for Critical Appraisal of Evidence:

  • Evidence is never perfect. It can be:

    • Incomplete
    • Misleading
    • Exaggerated
    • Based on weak information

  • Sometimes evidence looks strong, but is actually weak. For example:

    • A strong claim may be based on:

      • only one piece of information
      • a single unreliable source

    • A colleague’s confident opinion may be based on:

      • only an anecdote
      • limited personal experience

    • A long-used organizational practice may:

      • never have been properly tested or evaluated
      • be based on outdated assumptions

  • Therefore, not all evidence should be accepted at face value, and evidence must be carefully and systematically evaluated.

Key Questions of Evidence Appraisal:

  • Where did the evidence come from?
  • How was the evidence gathered?
  • Is it the best available evidence?
  • Is there enough evidence to support a conclusion?
  • Could the evidence be biased?

Appraising Different Types of Evidence

  1. Personal / Experiential Evidence

    • How many times has this person faced this issue?
    • Were the situations similar to the current one?
    • Is the experience broad enough to be useful?

  2. Organizational Evidence

    • How were the figures calculated?
    • Are the numbers accurate?
    • Are they reliable?
    • Are they complete and meaningful?

  3. Scientific Evidence

    • How was the study designed?
    • How were the data collected?
    • How was the outcome measured?
    • Are there alternative explanations for the result?

docs.title: (2) Focusing on the Best Available Evidence
docs.text:
Focusing on the best available evidence means:

  • In most situations, there is more than one type of evidence available
  • The challenge is not just collecting evidence, but deciding which evidence should we trust the most?
  • The quality of decisions improves when we use the most trustworthy evidence available
  • In other words: Better evidence makes better decisions

Reasons for Focusing on the Best Available Evidence:

  • Different sources of evidence are not equally convincing

  • Some evidence is:

    • weak
    • limited
    • uncertain

  • Other evidence is:

    • stronger
    • more systematic
    • more trustworthy

Examples of stronger vs weaker evidence:

  • If you want to know which holiday destination in Ireland has the least chance of rain in early August:

    • The most trustworthy evidence would be rainfall statistics, not a colleague’s personal memory from visiting once
    • Systematic data is usually more trustworthy than isolated personal experience

  • If a hospital wants to know whether Six Sigma can reduce medical errors:

    • Stronger evidence would come from a study of 150 European university hospitals measuring medical errors before and after implementation
    • This would be more trustworthy than one colleague’s experience in a single small hospital

However, sometimes the ideal high-quality evidence does not exist

  • For some decisions:

    • there may be no strong scientific evidence
    • there may be little or no organizational data

  • When strong evidence is missing, decision-makers may need to rely on:

    • professional experience
    • case studies
    • pilot testing
    • trial-and-error learning

  • However:

    • This evidence should still be used carefully
    • Its limitations should be recognized

docs.title: 4. Common Misunderstandings about Evidence-Based Practice
docs.text:
Misconceptions are a major barrier to adopting evidence-based practice (EBP)

Misconceptions usually come from:

  • Limited understanding
  • Oversimplified views of EBP

docs.title: (1) Misconception 1: EBP ignores professional experience
docs.text:
Misunderstanding: EBP only values research and ignores practitioners’ experience

Reality: EBP uses multiple sources of evidence, including experiential evidence (professional experience)

Key Points

  • No single type of evidence is always superior

  • Professional experience is valuable when:

  • it is critically appraised

  • it is relevant and trustworthy

  • Experience helps:

    • interpret other types of evidence
    • adapt decisions to specific contexts

Important conclusion about experience:

  • Deep specialized experience is more reliable
  • Unrelated or shallow experience is less reliable

docs.title: (2) Misconception 2: EBP is all about numbers and statistics
docs.text:
Misunderstanding: EBP = only quantitative data and statistics

Reality: EBP includes:

  • qualitative evidence
  • experience
  • stakeholder input
  • not just numbers

Key Points

  • You do not need to be a statistician
  • But you should understand basic concepts:
  • sample size
  • confidence intervals
  • effect sizes

  • statistical vs practical significance

  • EBP is about statistical thinking, not doing complex statistics

docs.title: (3) Misconception 3: Managers don’t have time for EBP
docs.text:
Misunderstanding: Decisions must be made quickly, so EBP is impractical

Reality:

  • EBP often involves:

    • Preparation before decisions
    • Reflecting on evidence quality

  • Most management decisions:

  • are not instant

  • take weeks or months

Key Points:

  • Even fast decisions require reliable evidence

  • Good decision-makers:

    • anticipate what evidence will be needed
    • prepare in advance

  • Time is not usually a barrier - EBP can actually improve both speed and quality of decisions

docs.title: (4) Misconception 4: Every organization is unique, so research doesn’t apply
docs.text:
Misunderstanding: Our organization is different, so scientific evidence is useless

Reality: Organizations are not identical, but not completely unique either

Key Points

  • Many management problems are repeated across organizations

  • Organizations often respond in similar ways

  • Good practitioners adapt general evidence to their specific context, rather than rejecting it completely

docs.title: (5) Misconception 5: Without high-quality evidence, nothing can be done
docs.text:
Misunderstanding: If strong evidence is not available, decision-making must stop

Reality:

  • Sometimes, high-quality evidence does not exist

  • In such cases, practitioners should:

    • use the best available evidence
    • even if it is limited

Key Approach

  • Use pilot testing, experimentation, learning by doing, etc.
  • Treat actions as prototypes
  • Continuously test, evaluate, and improve

docs.title: (6) Misconception 6: Good evidence gives you the answer
docs.text:
Misunderstanding: Evidence directly tells you what decision to make

Reality: Evidence is not an answer - It does not speak for itself

Key Points:

  • Evidence requires:

    • Interpretation
    • Context
    • Critical thinking

  • For example, A score (e.g., 10 points) is meaningless without knowing the average or understanding the context

  • Evidence is

    • not conclusive
    • not absolute truth
    • often uncertain

  • EBP helps you make better-informed decisions but does not guarantee a perfect answer

docs.title: Topic 1 - Data & Business Decision Making
docs.text:
Topic 1 provides a comprehensive foundation for understanding how data drives business decision making in modern organizations. The formal data analysis and management tools like SQL and relational databases are also covered in this topic.

The detailed learning objectives for this topic are:

Topic 1.1 - Data Analysis & Decision Making:

  • Understand the role of data analysis in supporting informed business decisions.
  • Familiar with the data analytical process: data wrangling & data analyzing and reporting.
  • Familiar with analytical levels: descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive analytics.

Topic 1.2 - Database Systems:

  • Understand the role of relational database systems in managing and storing data.
  • Understand key concepts of entity relationships: entity-relationship modeling, primary and foreign keys, and cardinality.
  • Familiar with reading and explaining entity-relationship diagrams (ERDs).

Topic 1.3 - SQL:

  • Know the basic structure and functions of SQL.
  • Familiar with basic data retrieval using SQL.
  • Understand special considerations in SQL queries, such as handling null values.

Topic 1.4 - Data Quality:

  • Know the importance of data quality in decision making.
  • Familiar with evaluating data relevance and reliability.
  • Understand the trade-offs between data precision and utility.

docs.title: Unit 1 - Data Analysis for Decision Making
1. Data Analysis: Data to Information
docs.text:
Data:

  • Unorganized raw facts
  • Any sequence of one or more symbols without context or meaning

Information:

  • Processed and organized data
  • Presented within a given context that is useful to humans
  • Given meaning by specific act of interpretation involving human judgement

docs.title: 2. Data Analysis & Decision Making
docs.text:
How data support decision making:

Demonstration: Data Supporting Decision Making

Citation: Jean Francois Puget:

The purpose of an analytics solution is to enable decisions based on data.

It does not necessarily mean that such solutions must compute decisions.

It means that whatever their output, they must support decision making.

In short, analytics is a journey from data to decisions and actions, via the use of many different techniques and tools.

docs.title: Unit 2 - Data Analytical Process: Data Wrangling & Analyzing & Reporting
docs.text: Data Analytical Process Overview: An Iterative & Repetitive Process:

docs.title: 1. Data Wrangling
docs.text:
Data wrangling is everything you do except analyse the data, so that you can analyse the data.

Demonstration: Time & Efforts in Data Analysis Stages

Citation: Gil Press:

Data scientists spend 60% of their time on cleaning and organizing data

Collecting data sets comes second at 19% of their time

80% of their time on preparing and managing data for analysis

Demonstration: Data Analytical Process

Demonstration: Data Visualization as an Iterative Process

Demonstration: Enterprise Data Pipeline

docs.title: (1) Data Analysis Trifecta: Data + Intent + Tools & Technologies
docs.text:
(a) Data

Data analysis project involve sourcing, exploring, and evaluating data:

  • Data analytics project may not begin with a pre-supplied dataset

  • Efforts must be made in exercising judgement over:

    • Which data is reliable & relevant
    • What weighting it should be given when making decision

(b) Intent

Data Analytical Intent:

  • Gain: Gain insight about what is happening in the world around us
  • Understand: Understand how we can influence what happens
  • See: See trends or patterns in activity and behavior
  • Predict: Predict events and outcomes
  • Set: Set goals and measure events and outcomes against those goals
  • Take: Take actions that lead to desired outcomes and achievement of goals

Two important feature of data analytical process:

  1. Data analysis requires being familiar with the specific context of your data analysis project:

    • Start a new analytics project:

      • Understand the desired business outcome and how it will be measured
      • Understand the decisions in scope that influence this outcome
      • Access the sponsorship who can assist you with this understanding

    • Manage sustained project engagement: prototyping, iterating, and getting feedback from users

      • Help develop a useful, relevant and more likely to be adopted solution
      • Ensures that the solution aligns with real user needs

    • Use specific examples

      • Illustrate the decision and context within which it is to be made
      • Reveal additional factors, goals, and strategies that also influence the decision
      • Be wary of over-solving the example instead of developing generalized approach

  2. Data analysis is a time-consuming and costly process

    • Producing a fully automated analytical solution is costly

      • Require deep understanding of the decision making context
      • Require consensus among all the incumbent decision makers

    • The analytical output is expected to be recommendations not facts or binding mandate

    • Not as simple or effortless as the buzzwords and marketing in data analysis, for example:

      • Rules-based engine,
      • Real-time factors and triggers,
      • Just give us access to your information...

(c) Tools & Technologies

Tools & technologies need to be guided by specific purpose, to produce something useful.

Demonstration: Computational Thinking

Citation: Denning, Peter J & Tedre, Matti (2021):

Computational Thinking: A Disciplinary Perspective, Informatics in Education:

Computational thinking is the mental skills and practices for designing computations that get computers to do jobs for us, and for explaining and interpreting the world in terms of information processes.

Citation: www.freecodecamp.org:

Generalized Problem-solving skills are almost unanimously the most important qualification that employers look for.

Understand -> Plan -> Divide & Combine

Relevant to other activities, not just computer programming, e.g., research projects, other disciplines.

docs.title: (2) Analytical Levels
docs.text:
Analytical Levels Concepts:

  • Analysts build solutions to aids decision maker from data to insight, to decision, and to action

  • Analytical levels describes:

    • How far the analyst pursues this journey
    • How many works left to decision makes to complete this journey

Analytical Levels Definition:

  • (1) Descriptive:

    • What happened or is happening?
    • Perspective on the data as is

  • (2) Diagnostic:

    • Why did it happen?
    • Insight about patterns or relationships

  • (3) Predictive:

    • What will happen?
    • Predict future events based on patterns or relationships

  • (4) Prescriptive:

    • What should we do?
    • Recommendations or actions that influence the future

Analytical Levels Comments:

  • Four analytical levels are overlapping rather than separate

  • The different levels depend on:

    • What is automated analytics work (automation is imitating human judgement)
    • What is left to additional human effort and judgement

  • Data analysis is the ongoing process of turning data into decisions (pushing arrow right)

    • Great deal of human effort and judgement is required
    • Either by an analyst, or collective wisdom captured into rules and calculations

Demonstration: Analytical Levels

In the context of analyzing sales:

(1) Descriptive - What happened?

  • Summarizes past sales, e.g., revenue, units sold
  • Breaks down by time, product, region, customer
  • Shows key KPIs and trends with charts

(2) Diagnostic - Why did it happen?

  • Analyzes sales by channel or location
  • Identifies causes of growth or decline
  • Explores customer behavior, returns, or inventory issues

(3) Predictive - What will happen?

  • Forecasts future sales using historical data
  • Uses models, e.g., time series, regression
  • Helps plan for demand, promotions, and budgets

(4) Prescriptive - What should we do?

  • Recommends actions based on predictions
  • Plans inventory, production, and staffing
  • Aims to reduce costs and optimize operations

docs.title: 1. Database Key Terminology
docs.text:
Data: Any sequence of one or more symbols given meaning by specific acts of interpretation

Metadata: Data that provides information about other data

  • Descriptive Metadata: a resource for purposes such as discovery and identification, e.g.,:

    • Name
    • Creator
    • File / data format

  • Structural Metadata: how data is organized, e.g.,:

    • Columns names and data types of a table
    • Relationships between tables

  • Administrative Metadata: when and how it was created, and who can access it, e.g.,:

    • Creation date
    • Last modified date
    • Access permissions

Database: An organized collection of data:

  • Generally stored and accessed electronically from a computer system
  • We decide how the data is organized after defining the metadata

Database Management System (DBMS): Software application that provides a user interface

  • Encompasses the core facilities provided to administer the database
  • Interacts with end users, other software, and the database itself
  • Facilitate access to the information in the database
  • Help store, retrieve, modify, and analyze the data

  • Hides the deep internal organization of database, specific SQL database format:

    • MS SQL Server / Azure SQL Database
    • Oracle
    • MySQL
    • PostgreSQL

Database System: The database and database management system together

docs.title: 1. Relational Database & DBMS
docs.text:
Relational DBMS enforces how data is stored and structures the based on business rules, through:

  • Unique fields (PK) to identify entity
  • Referencing fields (FK) to describe entity relationships
  • Required fields
  • Data type, size, and range

Relational DBMS Key Terminology:

  • Row / Record / Case: A single entry that stores information about a specific event or object, e.g., a customer, an order, a product
  • Column / Field / Attribute: An individual piece of information within a record, representing a specific attribute
  • Table / Entity: A structured collection of records that share the same set of fields

  • Structure: The defined format of a table enforced by the DBMS

    • Field names
    • Data types & size (text / number / date)
    • Allowed values
    • NULL rules

  • Schema: A group of contextually related tables that together represent a data model for a business

Reasons for Using Relational Database:

  • Better define the structure to enhance meaning, reduce redundancy, and improve data quality
  • Provide standardized interface (SQL) for defining, creating, modifying and retrieving data
  • Provide ease of access to data
  • Provide security controls and safeguard against loss and theft of data
  • Help maintain audit trails
  • Provide an integrated, enterprise-wide data repository as the single source of record

docs.title: 2. Normalization
docs.text:
Normalization: Dividing One Big Table to Multiple Tables

  • Normalization is the process of separating a single table into its many related component tables
  • Normalized schema is the resulting schema with multiple related component tables
  • Modern design of normalized schema is designed and documented using ERD

Demonstration: Relational Database: Normalization

docs.title: (1) Key
docs.text:
Key: A field or a set of fields that uniquely identifies a record

For example: In a table of students, the following fields can be used as keys:

  • Student ID Number
  • Citizen ID Number
  • Social Insurance Number

docs.title: (2) Primary Key & Alternative Key
docs.text:
Primary Key & Alternate Keys

  • Defined as part of the metadata
  • Create rules that the database will enforce to ensure uniqueness

Primary Key (PK): Key we have chosen to uniquely identify each record of a table

  • Primary keys must:

    • Have unique & known values - cannot be NULL
    • Cannot change over time
    • Should involve the fewest number of fields as possible

  • Natural Key vs Surrogate Key

    • Natural Key: selected from known facts
    • Surrogate Key: invented or designed for the database

Alternative Key (AK): Keys other than primary key

For example: In a table of students:

  • If Student ID Number is set as PK
  • Then, Citizen ID Number and Social Insurance Number are AKs

docs.title: (3) Foreign Key
docs.text:
Foreign key (FK): Non-key field in a table that references the primary key of another table

  • Foreign keys facilitate relationships between tables
  • DBMS will preserve and enforce the validity of the linked values

  • For example: A refer B:

    • Cannot insert or update a record in A with a foreign key that does not exist in B
    • Cannot delete a record in the B, unless all the records referencing it are deleted from A

Demonstration: Primary Keys & Foreign Keys

docs.title: 1. ERD Concepts
docs.text:
Definition of ERD: A semantic, graphical data model about how stored information is structured

  • Design and document database schema
  • Picture characteristics and relationships of entities (people, places, objects, events, concepts)
  • Expresses business rules as defined by the structure of the database

Reasons for using ERD: Provides documentation about the database

  • ERD is a technology independent tool for business people and IT people to communicate
  • ERD can results in a normalized schema if designed properly - revising poorly structured databases after software written or data recorded wastes time money

docs.title: 2. Cardinality
docs.text: Cardinality: Numerical relationship between occurrences of one entity and occurrences of the other

docs.title: (1) Unidirectional Relationship
docs.text:
Maximum vs Minimum Cardinality:

  • Maximum Cardinality: maximum number of relationships occurrences

    • Maximum One (At most, can have one occurrence)
    • Maximum Many (At most, can have many occurrences)

  • Minimum Cardinality: minimum number relationship relationships occurrence

    • Minimum Zero (Optional: At least, can have zero occurrences)
    • Minimum One (Required: At least, must have at least one occurrence)

Crow’s foot notation:

  • In Theory:

  • In Practice:

  • On the many side, we belive the minimum is always zero, therefore we only need to specify the maximum cardinality.

docs.title: (2) Bidirectional Relationship
docs.text:
1. One-To-One:

Considering maximum cardinality: One-to-one relationship between A & B means:

  • One occurrence of A is related to at most one occurrence of B
  • One occurrence of B is related to at most one occurrence of A

Considering minimum cardinality: Specifically:

  • One Required & One Optional: PK of optional side becomes FK on required side
  • Two Required: FK can be on either side
  • Two Optional: FK can be on either side

Demonstration: One-To-One Relationship

One Required & One Optional

One-to-one relationship between sales order and invoice:

  • One sales order is related to at most one & at least zero invoice
  • One invoice is related to at most one & at least one sales order

Two Required

One-to one relationship between employee and employee card:

  • One employee can have at most one & at least one employee card
  • One employee card can belong to at most one & at least one employee

Two Optional

One-to one relationship between student and locker:

  • One student can have at most one & at least zero locker
  • One locker can belong to at most one & at least zero student

2. One-To-Many:

Considering maximum cardinality: One-to-many relationship between A & B means:

  • One occurrence of A is related to at most many occurrences of B
  • One occurrence of B is related to at most one occurrence of A

Considering minimum cardinality: Specifically:

  • Optional One-To-Many: One occurrence on the "Many" side is related to at least zero occurrence on the "One" side
  • Require One-To-Many: One occurrence on the "Many" side is related to at least one occurrence on the "One" side

In all cases of one-to-many relationship:

  • PK on the "one" side becomes a FK on the "many" side
  • PK is always on the "one" side & FK is always on the "many" side

Demonstration: One-To-Many Relationship

Optional One-To-Many:

One-to-many relationship between customer and sales order:

  • One customer can have at most many sales orders
  • One sales order can belong to at most one and at least zero customer

Require One-To-Many:

One-to-many relationship between supplier and purchase order:

  • One supplier can have at most many purchase orders
  • One purchase order can belong to at most one and at least one supplier

3. Many-To-Many:

Considering maximum cardinality: Many-to-many relationship between A & B means:

  • One occurrence of A is related to at most many occurrences of B
  • One occurrence of B is related to at most many occurrences of A

However, minimum cardinality in a many-to-many relationship is not usually specified, because:

  • Many-to-many relationships cannot be implemented directly in a relational database
  • Many-to-many relationships must be divided to two One-To-Many relationships through associative entity
  • The PKs of the two related entities become the combined PKs of the associated entity

In terms of relationship between single entity and the associative entity:

  • Single entity is on the "one" side of the relationship with the associative entity, with minimum cardinality always being one
  • Associative entity is on the "many" side of the relationship with the single entity, with minimum cardinality not considered

Demonstration: Many-To-Many Relationship

Many-to-many relationship between teacher and subject:

  • One teacher can teach at most many subjects
  • One subject can be taught by at most many teachers

One-to-many relationship between teacher and teacher-subject:

  • One teacher can have at most many entries in teacher-subject table
  • One entry in teacher-subject table is related to at most one and at least one teacher

One-to-many relationship between subject and teacher-subject:

  • One subject can have at most many entries in teacher-subject table
  • One entry in teacher-subject table is related to at most one and at least one subject

Many-to-many relationship between doctor and patient:

  • One doctor can treat at most many patients
  • One patient can be treated by at most many doctors

One-to-many relationship between doctor and appointment:

  • One doctor can have at most many appointments
  • One appointment is related to at most one and at least one doctor

One-to-many relationship between patient and appointment:

  • One patient can have at most many appointments
  • One appointment is related to at most one and at least one patient

docs.title: (3) Special Relationships
docs.text:
1. Unary Relationships:

Unary relationship means that an entity can refer itself:

  • The PKs and FKs are on the same table
  • Unary relationships can be one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many (through an associative entity)

Demonstration: Unary Relationship

Unary One-To-One

Unary One-To-Many

Unary Many-To-Many (through an associative entity)

2. Referencing with Multiple Foreign Keys to Same Table

Referencing with multiple foreign keys to the same table means that:

  • Two different FKs in the same table reference the same PK in another table
  • This is similar to many-to-many unary relationship with associative entity

Demonstration: Referencing with Multiple Foreign Keys to Same Table

3. One-To-One or One-To-Many using Association Entity

In many-to-many relationships, we use an associative entity:

  • However, we can also use an associative entity to implement one-to-one or one-to-many relationships
  • In this case, we ususally want to capture some attributes of the relationship, which is not possible to capture in a direct relationship between two entities

Demonstration: One-To-One or One-To-Many using Association Entity

One-To-One using Association Entity

One-To-Many using Association Entity

4. Ternary Relationship:

Ternary Relationship means many-To-Many among three entities through association entity

  • This is similar to many-to-many relationship between two entities with associative entity
  • The PKs of the three related entities become the combined PKs & FKs of the associated entity

Demonstration: Ternary Relationship

docs.title: (1) ERD Models
docs.text:
ERD Models:

  • Conceptual Model: Overall Scope

    • Include general entities
    • Include high-level relationships

  • Logical Model: General ERD

    • Specify operational and transactional data entities
    • Include fields for each entity are identified
    • Identify keys, primary keys, and foreign keys for each entity

  • Physical Model: Specific ERD (ready for implementation)

    • Map entities to database tables
    • Specific data types and sizes of each field

Reasons for Classifying ERD Models

  • Design and document data models at different levels of abstraction
  • Different audiences have different needs for different levels of detail (managers, analyst, IT)
  • Good modelling process starts at the highest level of abstraction (conceptual) and work down towards the detail (logical & physical)

docs.title: (2) Technical Consideration vs Business Consideration
docs.text:
The structure and logic of the database enforce the model of database:

  • Choice of entities, attributes, relationships and associated cardinalities
  • Modeling correctly when designing the database is important
  • Subsequent changes can be risky and costly, which may introduce other problems

Key consideration: model should support the operating and reporting needs of the organization

  • This is not a technical issue, while there are technical aspects
  • This is a business issue and essential to the business
  • This should be made with active involvement from people who understand the business

docs.title: 1. SQL Basic Concepts
docs.text:
SQL (Structured Query Language): a computer language designed for interact with databases

SQL Basic Functions:

  • SQL DDL: Data Definition Language

    • Table Create
    • Table Update
    • Table Delete

  • SQL DML: Data Manipulation Language

    • Data Create
    • Data Update
    • Data Delete
    • Data Retrieve

Example: SQL Basic Functions

-- SQL DDL
-- Table Create
CREATE TABLE students (ID INT, Name VARCHAR(50))
-- Table Update
ALTER TABLE students ADD COLUMN Grade VARCHAR(2)
-- Table Delete
DROP TABLE students

-- SQL DML
-- Data Create
INSERT INTO students (ID, FirstName, LastName) VALUES (1234, 'Jane', 'Smith');
-- Data Update
UPDATE students SET Grade = 'H2' WHERE ID = 1234;
-- Data Delete
DELETE FROM students WHERE ID = 1234;
-- Data Retrieve
SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM students WHERE Grade = 'H1';

SQL is composed of three core elements: keywords, functions, and metadata

  • Keywords & Functions

    • Partly are same across all SQL DBMS
    • Partly are vendor-specific: MS SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL

  • Metadata: map of the database

docs.title: 2. SQL for Informed Decision Making
docs.text:
Reporting Solution: Passive Data & Information Consumption:

Reporting Solution: Flexible Access with SQL:

docs.title: Unit 2 - SQL Basics
docs.text: Please refer to the SQL Basics course through this link.

docs.title: Unit 3 - Null Values in SQL
docs.text:
Null Values: No value

  • Null value often happen when:

    • Data is missing
    • Data has not been captured yet (e.g. student pending graduation date)
    • Data is not applicable or not provided (e.g. missing middle name)

  • Common mistakes on null values

    • Null values is not 0
    • Null values is not empty text

Null Value Calculations:

  • Identify Null Value: IS NULL or IS NOT NULL

  • Numerical & Logical Calculation: Also yields null value

    • e.g., 1 + NULL produces NULL
    • e.g., True AND NULL produces NULL

  • Aggregate Functions:

    • COUNT(*): Consider Null Value
    • COUNT(Col) / SUM(Col) / AVG(Col) / MAX(Col) / MIN(Col): Ignore Null value

docs.title: Unit 1 - Data Quality: Relevance & Reliability
docs.text:
Relevance & Reliability:

  • Relevance: How suitable is the data for the decision or analysis purpose?
  • Reliability: How trustworthy is the data for the decision or analysis purpose?

docs.title: (1) Evidence-Based Management
docs.text:
Evidence-based management is about making decisions through the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of the best available evidence from multiple sources.

Evidence-Based Management: Six-A Framework: Six steps to increase the likelihood of a favorable outcome:

  • Ask: Translate a practical issue or problem into an answerable question
  • Acquire: Systematically search for and retrieve evidence
  • Appraise: Critically judge the trustworthiness and relevance of the evidence
  • Aggregate: Weigh and pull together the evidence
  • Apply: Incorporate the evidence into to the decision-making process
  • Assess: Evaluate the outcome of the decision taken

docs.title: (2) PICOC Framework
docs.text:
PICOC Framework: Acquire and appraise the best available relevant evidence

  • Population / Problem, e.g., Health-conscious young consumers
  • Intervention / Success Factor, e.g., Launching a new high-protein cereal flavor
  • Comparison, e.g., Existing best-selling flavor, from our own or competing brands
  • Outcome or Objective, e.g., Improved sales
  • Context, e.g., Sales channels, locations, ...

docs.title: (3) Recency vs Currency
docs.text:
Recency & Currency (not considered in PICOC Framework)

  • Recency: Whether data is fresh: Late or outdated data can negatively affect decisions

    • e.g., A pizza order recorded an hour late breaks the 30-minute guarantee.
    • e.g., 1-hour-old data might be OK for illiquid stocks, but not for high-frequency trading

  • Currency: Whether data still reflects the current reality.

    • e.g., address
    • e.g., job title

  • Best practice:

    • Prefer recording stable facts (e.g., date of birth) rather than changing values (e.g., age)
    • Include timestamps in the dataset to help analysts assess recency and currency

docs.title: 2. Data Reliability
docs.text: Data Reliability Attributes:

docs.title: Unit 2 - Data Quality: Precision vs Utility
1. Accuracy vs Precision
docs.text:
Different concepts: a number may be precise but inaccurate or imprecise but accurate

  • Accuracy: How close a value is to the actual or true value.
  • Precision: How detailed or exact a value is (e.g., number of decimal places).

Same efforts or accuracy & precision: Difficult to collecting more accurate or more precise data:

  • Requires more effort, better tools, and higher costs
  • Does not always lead to better decisions

docs.title: 2. Precision vs Utility
docs.text:
False sense of accuracy and reliability: People assume precise numbers are more trustworthy:

  • Overprecision can actually hinder understanding by adding noise.
  • Use more meaningful figures in communication: e.g., $6.75M instead of $6,745,098.25
  • Use significance-based formatting to indicate uncertainty or estimation
  • Do not provide a highly precise number unless it adds real value

docs.title: Topic 2 Extension 1 - Financial Times Visual Vocabulary
Topic 2 Extension 2 - Evergreen’s Data Visualization Checklist
1. Introduction
docs.text:
Purpose: This checklist is used as a guide for the development of high impact data visualizations

Scope:

  • Only suitable to quantitative data visualizations: bar charts, line charts, pie charts etc.
  • Not suitable for non-quantitative plots: tree diagram, flow chart, logic model, maps, photos etc.

Scoring System:

  • Score Levels:

    • 2 = Fully met
    • 1 = Partially met
    • 0 = Not met
    • N/A = Not applicable, e.g., pie charts don’t have x/y axes

  • Score Target:

    • Maximum: 48 points (adjusted if NA applies)
    • Excellent visualizations: 80-90% (approximately 38 - 43 points)

docs.title: (1) Text
docs.text:
Overall Principles:

  • Graphs don't contain much text.
  • Existing text must encapsulate your message and pack a punch.

docs.title: (2) Arrangement
docs.text:
Overall Principles:

  • Improper arrangement of graph elements can confuse readers at best and mislead viewer at worst.
  • Thoughtful arrangement makes a data visualization easier for a viewer to interpret.

docs.title: (3) Color
docs.text:
Overall Principles:

  • Keep culture-laden color connotations in mind, e.g., pink is associated with feminine qualities in USA.
  • Use sites like Color Brewer to find color schemes suitable for black-and-white print and for colorblindness.

docs.title: (4) Lines
docs.text:
Overall Principles:

  • Excessive lines (gridlines, borders, tick marks, and axes) can add clutter or noise to a graph
  • So eliminate excessive lines whenever they aren’t useful for interpreting the data.

docs.title: (5) Overall
docs.text:
Overall Principles:

  • Graphs will catch a viewer’s attention so only visualize the data that needs attention.
  • Too many graphics of unimportant information dilute the power of visualization.

docs.title: Topic 2 - Data Visualization
docs.text:
This topic focuses on the principles and practices of data visualization. It covers the basic concepts of visualization, the use of visualization tools like Tableau, and the evaluation of visualizations for effectiveness and clarity. The detailed learning objectives for this topic are:

docs.title: Unit 1 - Data Visualization Definition and Purpose
1. Definition of Data Visualization
docs.text:
Definition of Data Visualization (Stephen Few, 2014): Data Visualization is:

  • Graphical display of abstract information for sense-making, understanding, or data analysis
  • Fundamental output from the visual analytics process

docs.title: 2. Purpose of Data Visualization
docs.text:
Reasons for Data Visualization:

  • People make better decisions based on understanding, rather than feeling or best guess

  • Vision is the most powerful sense of human: provides most effective understanding

    • Humans have extraordinary visual capacity to detect patterns, trends, and outliers
    • Information in visual form can be understood more quickly, reliably, and consistently

  • Data visualization is useful for:

    • Discovering data: exploration and understanding
    • Communicating insights in data
    • Making better informed decisions

Demonstration: Anscombe’s Quartet

In the following 4 scenarios:

  • The data has same statistical properties: size, mean, median, variance, regression coefficients
  • The data shows different perceptions in their scatter plots

Combined use of graphs and statistical methods in data analysis to better perceive:

  • Patterns, trends, exceptions
  • Appropriateness of varied prediction models

docs.title: 3. Data Visualization Process
docs.text:
Data visualization is an iterative and non-linear cycle (Steps may be skipped, repeated, or restarted):

  • Identify questions
  • Acquire evidence and data
  • Select visual structures
  • Create data views
  • Analyze, synthesize, and build hypotheses
  • Share findings and re-examine

docs.title: 1. Data Visualization Intent Categories
docs.text:
Data visualization can be classified into 3 categories by different intents:

  1. Explanatory

    • Explain something to others
    • Communicate understanding or conclusions from the data
    • Convince, recommend, or support decisions

  2. Exploratory

    • Extract information from unfamiliar data
    • Answer questions
    • Generate hypotheses

  3. Confirmatory

    • Test a pre-existing hypothesis
    • Find evidence to support or reject the hypothesis

docs.title: 2. Relationship between Three Intent Categories
docs.text:
These three categories are not mutually exclusive

  • They often occur in sequences or iterations as more data is acquired

  • Typical Sequences:

    • Hypothesis → Confirm → Explain
    • Purpose → Explore → Explain
    • Purpose → Explore → Hypothesis → Confirm → Explain
    • Purpose → Explore → Hypothesis → Reject
    • Purpose → Explore → Hypothesis
    • Purpose → Explore → Hypothesis → Predict → Confirm

docs.title: 3. Reasons for Categorizing Data Visualization Intents
docs.text:
Categorizing data visualization intents can:

  • Help focus the analysis and increase efficiency
  • Help prevent getting lost in vast amounts of data - avoid “forever exploring”
  • Help ensure that analysis results are aligned with business objectives
  • Help prevent over-reliance on tools or models while neglecting the actual business context

docs.title: Unit 1 - Principles for Effective Data Visualization
docs.text:
Effective Data Visualization:

  • Helps answer a well-framed valuable question
  • Uses data relevant to the question
  • Present the data in the best possible way to help answer the question

Accuracy of Quantitative Perceptual Task in Comparing Differences:

  • Accuracy of perception means perceiving differences & magnitude of differences among items
  • We do not perceive accurate and precise measurement of each items (already in data)

docs.title: Unit 2 - Instruction on Plot Types
docs.text:
Plots used in this subject:

  • Pie chart is not recommended
  • Bar chart (including histogram) & line chart are most commonly used - totally nearly 90%
  • Bullet chart is a special kind of bar chart that help you earn extra credit in assignment

Other plots that require statistical background of audience is not used:

  • Correlation matrix heat map
  • Box plot
  • Scatter plot with fitted regression line

docs.title: 1. Pie Charts
docs.text:
Pie chart is almost never the best choice - less effective than bar charts in comparing values

  • Limited effectiveness

    • Only present relative proportions - absolute values need to be labeled separately
    • Cannot be used in case of negative values
    • Hard to compare values over time - needs multiple pie charts per period
    • Relies heavily on color to distinguish categories - color cannot be used for other insights
    • Slices are dependent - increasing one slices shrinks other slices

  • Limited perception:

    • Hard to identify overall slices size or compare difference between slices sizes
    • Hard to identify difference between multiple pie charts
    • Misleading if lacking context - viewers wrongly assume larger is better (cost vs revenue)

Example: Pie Charts

Multiple pie charts for comparison across time

Negative values in pie charts

docs.text:
Bar Charts: More effective in comparing values between categories

docs.title: 1. Reasons for Evaluating the Plot Effectiveness
docs.text:
Data visualization should reliably support the analytic intent.

The impact of a low-quality visualization depends on analytic intent:

  • Exploratory: may slow down or mislead exploration
  • Confirmatory: may incorrectly confirm or reject a hypothesis
  • Explanatory: may fail to communicate insight - the audience confused or unconvinced

docs.title: 2. Plot Evaluating Tools & Resources:
docs.text:
Main Tools: Junk Charts Trifecta Check-Up

  • Three pillars of a good chart:

    • (1) What is the practical question?
    • (2) What does the data say?
    • (3) What does the chart say?

  • Data visualization must align all three:

    • (1) Choose relevant data
    • (2) Design clear visual elements that directly support the question
    • (3) Eliminate noise and ensure everything contributes to answering the core question

docs.title: Topic 2.3 - Designing Interactive Dashboards & Periodic Reports
Unit 1 - Interactive Dashboards vs Periodic Reports
1. Definition of Interactive Dashboard
docs.text:
Interaction:

  • Obtain additional detail on demand
  • Enables the user to explore beyond the original display of information

Dashboard:

  • Visual display of the most important information needed to achieve one or more objectives
  • Consolidated and arranged on a single screen - information can be monitored at a glance

docs.title: 2. Different Purposes & Audiences of Interactive Dashboard
3. Dashboard Sketching
docs.text:
Dashboard Sketching before Implementing:

  • Manages complexity - break down complexity into simple elements.
  • Supports collaboration - separates Explore & Design from Build & Test.
  • Fast and low-cost - easy to test ideas and get early feedback.
  • Encourages openness - promotes improvement and iteration.
  • Better layout planning - consider space and structure before using tools.
  • Keeps focus on purpose - avoid unnecessary decoration.
  • Prevents over-design - avoid adding “just-in-case” features.

docs.title: 4. Reasons for Interactive Dashboard - Two Meetings Scenario
docs.text:
Traditional Report-Based Meeting vs Dashboard-Driven Meeting:

(a) Traditional Report-Based Meeting (Meeting A)

  • Description:

    • You are about to go to a monthly strategy review meeting
    • Copies of individual departmental reports have been sent for review
    • You arrive, and each department head gives a 5-minute summary of their department’s activity and concerns. Most of the concerns raised are about how departments are not doing enough to support each other
    • There is much time spent arguing over discrepancies in numbers between departmental reports and defending the conclusions each department has made independently
    • The meeting concludes with a general feeling that little has been accomplished

  • Features:

    • Each department presents separate reports
    • Departments operate separately
    • Time spent defending numbers or finding discrepancies
    • Ends with confusion and lack of resolution

  • Illustration:

(b) Dashboard-Driven Meeting (Meeting B)

  • Description:

    • You are about to go to a monthly strategy review meeting
    • There is a well-designed set of dashboards linked to the company’s goals; built on top of shared, trusted data
    • You arrive, and a lead analyst gives a 5-minute overview of challenges the company is facing, new developments arising, and emerging opportunities - all easily identified in, and explained with, the dashboards
    • The rest of the meeting is spent discussing what the company can do to meet the identified challenges, monitor and mitigate new developments, or take advantage of emerging opportunities
    • The meeting concludes with everyone knowing what to do to keep company on course

  • Features:

    • One unified dashboard linked to shared data
    • Analyst summarizes key challenges and opportunities
    • Time spent discussing action, not just information
    • Clear outcomes and alignment by the end

  • Illustration:

Improvements from Meeting A to Meeting B

  • Technology

    • Necessary but not sufficient
    • Capture organization-wide data and build and deploy dashboards

  • Dashboards - well designed and aligned

    • The content and layout are designed to support the needs of the organization
    • The objectives and measures of performance are well defined, and agreed by all
    • The data to compute measures is centrally available, understood, and of good quality
    • The participants have been trained to interpret and interact with the dashboard

docs.title: Topic 3.1 - Python for General Purpose Programming
Unit 1 - Introduction to Python & Jupyter Notebook
1. Python & Jupyter Notebook
docs.text:
Python: A General Purpose Programming Language

  • General Purpose: can be used for many things. In data analysis, it is used for:

    • Wrangling data
    • Automating repetitive tasks
    • Machine learning and artificial intelligence

  • Most Popular: Widely used by technology companies globally:

    • Google & YouTube
    • Netflix
    • Amazon

  • Open Source:

    • Developed, managed, and maintained by the community & for the community
    • Freely usable by anyone for anything

  • Rich Ecosystem:

    • Large collection of libraries, toolsets, and frameworks
    • Good that someone has done what you are about to do already

  • Simple & Powerful Syntax:

    • Close to natural human language
    • Easier to learn and increases productivity

  • Still a Programming Language: Challenging for beginners

    • Computers only follow instructions: programmer should be clear on those instructions
    • Computers do not adapt to changing circumstances

Jupyter Notebook: A powerful way to write Python

  • Code organized into blocks: supports more convenient step-by-step execution

    • Easier to understand
    • Easier to explore and test

  • Store documentation (comments and markup) & outputs with code

  • Reusable environment: supports other languages — not only Python

    • R: Install IRkernel in R interpreter
    • SQL: Install ipython-sql in Python interpreter

  • Flexible tool for initial development, learning, teaching, and research

docs.title: 2. Data Analysis in Python
docs.text:
Benefits:

  • Repeatable and consistent
  • Auditable
  • Up front time investment, for continuous time saved returns each time we reuse

Usefulness:

  • Data wrangling into storage or further analysis
  • Repetitive / consistent / routine tasks
  • Well defined process / structure / rules
  • Complicated processes / rules
  • Computation-intensive tasks (require numerical / statistical output)

Limitations:

  • Changing context
  • Complex process requiring human judgement (e.g., Machine Learning and AI)

docs.title: 3. Python Leaning
docs.text:
Tips for Learning Python & Other Programming Languages

  • Learn by doing - construct your own code
  • Logic first, comment second, code last - don’t write any code before writing the algorithm
  • Piece by piece, step by step - explore and confirm interactively
  • Live with errors - better programmers are more curious about bugs & errors, than irritated
  • Google is your best friend, and ChatGPT your new friend - use to tutor, not plagiarize
  • Reuse reliable resources - use libraries, cheat sheets, and your own proven code
  • Success is mostly determined by utility - informative for decision making

docs.title: 1. Algorithms vs Program
docs.text:
Algorithms vs Program:

  • Algorithm: abstract description of how to perform a task

  • Program: specific description of how to perform a task written in a programming language

Example: Algorithms vs Program: Sorting a List

Algorithms: To sort a list, we can:

  • Firstly create a temporary empty list

  • Then, we iterate the input list. At each round:

    • Find the minimum item
    • Put it into the end of empty list
    • Remove it from the input list

  • After all rounds, we return the temporary list

Program (in Python):

def sort_list(input_list):
    temp_list = []
    working_list = input_list.copy()

    while working_list != []:
        min_val = min(working_list)
        temp_list.append(min_val)
        working_list.remove(min_val)

    return temp_list

docs.title: 2. Abstraction
docs.text:
Abstractions: Programming Components

  • Abstraction hides the details of how it works and makes you focus on what it does

  • Abstraction makes programmer not have to understand all the minutia of how tasks are done

  • Abstraction can also be built out of other abstractions

    • This is what makes modern software possible
    • This is how very complex-task programs are created

  • Typical abstraction techniques:

    • Functions: function(object, other_arguments)
    • Methods: object.method(other_arguments)

docs.title: 1. Dynamic String: string.format()
docs.text:
Example: Dynamic String: string.format()

Input:

n1 = "小明"
c1 = 1
p1 = "班长"

n2 = "张三"
c2 = 3
p2 = "学习委员"

s1 = "{}是{}班的{}"
print(s1.format(n1, c1, p1))
print(s1.format(n2, c2, p2))

Output:

小明是1班的班长
张三是3班的学习委员

Input:

s2 = "{0}是一位{2}，{0}所在的班级是{1}班"
print(s2.format(n1, c1, p1))
print(s2.format(n2, c2, p2))

Output:

小明是一位班长，小明所在的班级是1班
张三是一位学习委员，张三所在的班级是3班

docs.title: 2. Dynamic String: "f" strings
docs.text:
Example: Dynamic String: "f" strings

Input:

s3_1 = f"{n1}是{c1}班的{p1}"
s3_2 = f"{n2}是{c2}班的{p2}"

print(s3_1)
print(s3_2)

Output:

小明是1班的班长
张三是3班的学习委员

Input:

def get_formatted_string(n, c, p):
    return f"{n}是{c}班的{p}"

print(get_formatted_string(n1, c1, p1))
print(get_formatted_string(n2, c2, p2))

Output:

小明是1班的班长
张三是3班的学习委员

docs.title: 3. Comparing string.format() vs "f" strings
docs.text:
Advantages of Formatted Strings (Both string.format() and "f" Strings):

  • Easier to Maintain and Modify

    • Variables can be inserted directly
    • Avoid manual concatenation and reduce syntax errors

  • Improved Readability

    • Clearer and more structured format
    • Easier to read and understand at a glance

  • Less Error-Prone

    • Avoids complex concatenation
    • Reduces mistakes such as missing quotes or parentheses

  • Better Reusability

    • Templates can be reused with different variables
    • Code is more flexible and adaptable

  • Cleaner Syntax

    • No need for + operators or escapes
    • More natural and readable

Features of string.format():

  • Syntax:

    • Method available on string objects
    • Use {} placeholders
    • Supports positional and keyword arguments

  • Benefits:

    • Works even if variables are unknown at definition time
    • Supports flexible substitution and formatting (numbers, alignment)
    • Allows template reuse

  • Limitations:

    • Requires tracking of argument order
    • More verbose than "f" strings
    • Slightly harder to maintain for simple messages

Features of "f" string:

  • Syntax:

    • Prefix string with "f"
    • Directly insert variables inside {}

  • Benefits:

    • Concise and readable
    • Great for quick, one-time use
    • Good for repeated or simple substitutions
    • Useful for SQL queries or formatted output

  • Limitations:

    • Variables must be defined before use
    • Not reusable in loops if defined once
    • Less clear with complex expressions
    • Fewer advanced formatting options than string.format()

docs.title: Unit 2 - Pandas Methods Chain
docs.text:
Methods chaining in Pandas is a sequence of multiple operations applied consecutively on a DataFrame, for example:

(
    dfSales
    .groupby(['CatDescr', 'ProdDescr'])
    .SalesQuantity.sum()
    .reset_index()
)

In this example, multiple operations are chained together:

  • First, the DataFrame is grouped by 'CatDescr' and 'ProdDescr'
  • Then, the 'SalesQuantity' column is summed for each group
  • Finally, the index is reset to get a clean DataFrame

The advantage of method chaining include:

  • Improved readability and understandability of the code
  • Easier to debug and maintain
  • Reduces the need for intermediate variables
  • Note: the opening and closing parentheses are essential, otherwise it will result in a syntax error

If we use intermediate variables instead of method chaining, the code would be longer and less readable, for example:

dfSales2 = dfSales.groupby(['CatDescr', 'ProdDescr']).SalesQuantity.sum()
dfSales3 = dfSales2.reset_index()
dfSales3

docs.title: Unit 3 - Simulation with Python
docs.text:
Simulating from Distributions

  • Uniform Distribution: random.uniform(a, b)

    • Uniform distribution from a to b
    • Results are distributed evenly across the range [a, b]
    • Values cannot be smaller than a or larger than b

  • Normal Distribution: random.normalvariate(mu=a, sigma=b)

    • Normal distribution with mean μ = a and standard deviation σ = b
    • Values are distributed centrally around the mean
    • With small probability, values can be very large or very small (even negative)

Example: Distribution & Negative Numbers

Input:

pd.Series([random.uniform(1, 10) for i in range(100000)]).plot(kind='hist')

Output:

Histogram showing a uniform distribution between 1 and 10:

Input:

pd.Series([random.normalvariate(5, 20) for i in range(100000)]).plot(kind='hist')

Output:

Histogram showing a normal distribution with mean 5 and standard deviation 20

docs.title: Case Background: Communication with Air London
docs.text:
Narrator: The BSI team has been called in to help build a better rebooking engine for Air London, an airline that has been in business for a little over three years. In this case, you get to try out to be part of the BSI team and help us make some decisions based on data and analytics. Good luck.

Ian (AL): Irregularities in passenger handling at our hubs is hurting Air London's customer satisfaction ratings. In fact, this past quarter we were rated near the bottom of all European based airlines.

Jodice (BSI): Can you give me an example of a typical problem you'd like to resolve?

Ian (AL): Yes, here is one. Looks like we're going to have another misconnect situation at our Frankfurt hub. Four passengers from various locations connecting to our London flight will be landing in the next hour. They've all missed their original connections, but there are only two available seats on the last flight today.

Jodice (BSI): So you need to pick two to go and two to stay overnight or transfer to other airlines at a higher cost to you.

Ian (AL): Yes, except ours is the last flight of the day, so we're stuck.

Jodice (BSI): Sounds like it's time to overhaul Air London's rebooking app using a better rules based engine to include more real time factors and triggers. Give us access to your information systems and my team will come up with some fresh ideas about how to improve your rebookings.

docs.title: First-Round Selection Based on Original Factors
docs.text:
Narrator: Jodice turns the project over to Chi and Matt. They start by looking at passenger information for the Frankfurt to London misconnected situation.

Matt (BSI): The airline uses cameras at check in to capture passenger photos. Here's the impacted customer report. I just built to pull all the basic passenger info Air London uses today, but on a single screen to make our rebooking analysis faster.

Matt (BSI): Jason is flying from Cairo through Rome to Frankfurt and then heading to London. Cheap ticket, which I guess accounts for all the stops. He has more than 4,000 frequent flyer miles this year, 128k total.

Chi (BSI): Looks like Lana does a little bit of traveling too. We don't have any data about Steffi. She must be a first time flyer. Long trip for her trom Japan.

Matt (BSI): Check out Conrad. He's a big time Traveler. A Tier 1 customer with more than 260,000 lifetime miles with Air London. We need to keep an eye on him.

Narrator: Based on this basic data, which two passengers would you send to London?

docs.title: Second-Round Selection Based on New Factors
docs.text:
Narrator: To create deeper customer insights, Matt and Chi add new fields to the rebooking screen that contain additional information about each passenger from finance.

Matt (BSI): I’ve added some financial contribution scores including lifetime value predictions and current year revenues.

Chi (BSI): And these fields on profit and frequency of a Bookings show Jason only books the lowest margin flights. Lana books last minute but pays full fare, so she's very high margin. Plus she is booking more frequently. Seems like Conrad isn't a steady traveler, but it looks like his company's booking engine is forcing lower margin choices on him.

Matt (BSI): Based on this additional information, who do you think should go to London?

Narrator: Would you like to revise your two choices?

docs.title: Third-Round Selection Based on New Factors
docs.text:
Chi (BSI): Before we decide too quickly, it's important to consider some other factors we can add. Which booking channels people use, their costs, and other information about the use of those channels.

Chi (BSI): For example, Jason books on the web, cheap channel. But we can see from the notes that he also exits the Air London site to competitors. So, clearly he is price sensitive.

Matt (BSI): Well, look at Lana. She only book through the contact center, never online. My contact costs us more to serve, but we get additional info by analyzing call center logs. Looks like Steffi booked via a travel agent. And Conrad, he always uses his corporate web engine to book. That's low cost to Air London.

Narrator: Based on this additional channel report, do you want to change your selections?

docs.title: Final-Round Selection Based on New Factors
docs.text:
Narrator: Early the next morning.

Matt (BSI): Here's something I worked on last night. While we need to put all the factors into the rebooking engine, we also need to build a customer centric display. One that frontline people like gate agents can use, and to give them a bird's eye view of what's happening for each individual passenger, as well as how valuable the customer is. Here's a mock up.

Chi (BSI): I like it. Several different portlets of information: customer lifetime value, booking history, and weighted on how recently a passenger had issues.

Matt (BSI): Yes, when I was building that screen, I realized that there are operational real time factors that we could also add to the customer page.

Chi (BSI): Good thinking. What other kinds of active information goes into that part of the screen?

Matt (BSI): Well, for starters, it turns out Lana checked in with an infant in arms. And look, here's another negative factor. Bags from Rome didn't make the Frankfurt flight.

Chi (BSI): Poor Lana. Maybe the rules engine should give her a break. A baby, lost bags. At least she's going home to the UK if we send her there as part of the top two.

Matt (BSI): Ops. And here's another input from live contact center notes. Adding in calls to customer care while in route. Stephie's original flight from Japan was canceled. She waited six hours in Tokyo for her next flight. Look at these call logs. She is not happy.

Chi (BSI): I think we have a good handle on some factors for the new rule base. Let's bring Jodice up to speed right away.

Narrator: Based on these active factors. It's time to lock in your final choices.

docs.title: Solutions to the Mis-Connection Problem
docs.text:
Narrator: The team prepares their presentation and factors in one more new opportunity to do better rebooking.

Jodice (BSI): So what have you found?

Chi (BSI): There are a lot of factors that Air London can use to make better rebooking decisions. The good news is most of the information is readily accessible. It's a matter of loading it into their active data warehouse so it's all in one place and real time analytics can be run.

Matt (BSI): The real time information should give them a competitive edge since airlines have a lot of moving parts. Speaking of real time, we thought of one more opportunity. We read in the Times that Air London is adding in flight Internet seatback capabilities.

Chi (BSI): Our idea is to use pop up screens to interact with impacted customers, giving them options and gathering information. The system would interact with them in priority order based on the rebooking scoring. For example, we might find out that our top priority passenger, Conrad, would have been happy to take the flight to London around noon the next day.

Matt (BSI): That freed up a seat. Our number two choice, Jason, actually lives in Frankfurt. He'd be fine with canceling the last leg.

Jodice (BSI): So that means your number three and four choices would have made the last flight of the day?

Chi (BSI): Right. By having interactive capabilities, we would have accommodated Lana with the baby and Stuffy.

Jodice (BSI): Looks like everybody would be happy. Great work. I'll call Ian to describe how the system could have handled this Frankfurt scenario and see what he thinks of the new rebooking ideas.

Matt (BSI): Sure, no problem, chief. And when do I get promoted? I'm tired of carrying Chi.
