docs.title: 1. ERD of Airline Database
docs.text:
Conceptual Design:

Logical Design:

docs.title: (1) Cardinality Understanding
docs.text:
(a) What is the cardinality between aircraft and flight?

Optional one-to-many:

  • One flight can have at least zero and at most one plane assigned to it
  • One plane can be assigned to at least zero and at most many flights

(b) What is the cardinality between ticket and flight?

Required one-to-many:

  • One flight can have at least zero and at most many tickets
  • One ticket can have at least one and at most one flight

(c) What is the cardinality between flight and booking?

Optional many-to-many:

  • One flight can have at least zero and at most many bookings
  • One booking can have at least one and at most many flights

(d) What is the cardinality between Route and Airport?

The relations between Route and Airport are combined with two one-to-many relationships:

First one-to-many relationship:

  • One route can have at least one and at most one departure airport
  • One airport can be the departure airport for at least zero and at most many routes

Second one-to-many relationship:

  • One route can have at least one and at most one arrival airport
  • One airport can be the arrival airport for at least zero and at most many routes

(e) Which of the fields in the flight table do not allow null values?

In the flight table, the fields Flight_Number and Date do not allow null values. These are both part of the composite primary key, and since PKs uniquely identify records, the values must be known.

It is worth noting that Tail_Number does allow NULLs, because it is an optional FK. One flight can have at least zero and at most one plane assigned to it, so the Tail_Number can be NULL if no plane has been assigned.

For other field, i.e., Status, we do not have enough information in the ERD about it. It may or may not allow NULLs. It is reasonable to infer that it cannot be NULL since the airline would know the status of each of the flights it operates.

docs.title: (2) Business Understanding
docs.text:
Using the ERD above, explain whether each of the following business operations is supported by the model or not:

(a) Can a flight be scheduled before a plane has been assigned to it?

Yes. Since one flight can have at least zero and at most one plane assigned to it, the Tail_Number can be NULL if no plane has been assigned. This allows a flight to be scheduled before a plane has been assigned to it.

(b) Can a flight be oversold (more tickets than seats)? Can a flight be reassigned a different plane?

Yes, a flight can be oversold. To check whether a flight is oversold, we can count the number of tickets and compare that with the number of seats on the plane. However, simply looking at ERD, we cannot see whether there is restriction on this. So, we can infer that there is no such restriction, and a flight can be oversold.

Yes, a flight can be reassigned a different plane. To do this, we can simply update the Tail_Number in the flight table to a different one.

(c) Can a booking exist without any tickets?

No. From the conceptual design of ERD, one booking can have at least one and at most many tickets. Therefore, a booking cannot exist without any tickets.

(d) Can a ticket be issued independent of a booking?

No. Since one ticket is associated with at least one and at most one booking, a ticket cannot be issued without being associated with a booking, and Booking_Code is a required FK in the Ticket table.

(e) Can a booking be for more than one passenger? For more than one flight for the same passenger?

Yes, a booking can be for more than one passenger. A booking can have more than one ticket. Each ticket can have a different Passenger_Name.

Yes, a booking can be for more than one flight for the same passenger. A booking can have more than one ticket. Different tickets can have different Flight_Number, but the same Passenger_Name.

(f) Can a ticket be booked with an open date (i.e. known flight, but date chosen later)

No. One ticket is associated with at least one and at most one flight, and Date is part of the composite PK of the flight table, i.e., Date is a required FK in the Ticket table. Therefore, a ticket cannot be booked with an open date.

(g) Can a person join the rewards program before making a booking? Must all passengers be rewards members?

Yes, a person can join the rewards program before making a booking. The relationship between Ticket and Rewards_Member indicates that one reward member can have at least zero and at most many tickets. Since, one reward member can have at least zero tickets, it is possible for a person to join the rewards program before making a booking.

No, all passengers do not have to be rewards members. Since Rewards_Member is an optional FK in Ticket, therefore it can be NULL, which means that a passenger can be a non-rewards member. Therefore, not all passengers have to be rewards members.

docs.title: 3. SQL Queries Interpretation
docs.text:
What is the business intent behind, and usefulness of the data returned, by each of the following queries?

(a)

SELECT *
FROM Flight
WHERE Tail_Number IS NULL
  AND Date BETWEEN '2025-03-25' AND '2025-03-31' -- or any future week

This query finds all flights that are scheduled to operate in the future week but do not have a plane assigned to them yet.

This can be useful for the airline to identify flights that may need attention in terms of plane assignment, and to ensure that all flights have planes assigned before their scheduled departure dates.

(b)

SELECT
  Flight_Number,
   Date,
   COUNT(*) / c.Seats as Rate
FROM Flight f
  INNER JOIN Ticket t
    ON t.Flight_Number = f.Flight_Number
      AND t.Date = f.Date
  INNER JOIN Aircraft c
    ON c.Tail_Number = f.Tail_Number
WHERE Status = 'Scheduled'
GROUP BY f.Flight_Number, f.Date, c.Seats
HAVING Rate > 0.95
  OR Rate < 0.50
ORDER BY f.Date

This query calculates the booking rate for each scheduled flight by number of tickets sold divided by the total number of seats on the aircraft. It then filters for flights that are either over 95% booked or under 50% booked.

This information can be useful for identifying flights that are either very popular (overbooked) or not popular (underbooked). For overbooked flights, we can consider re-assigning a larger plane or planning more flights on the same route. For underbooked flights, we can consider re-assigning a smaller plane or merging flights on the same route to improve efficiency.

docs.title: 1. Background & ERD of HSX Database
docs.text:
The Hollywood Stock Exchange® (www.hsx.com) is the world's leading entertainment stock market. At HSX.com, registered traders buy and sell virtual shares of celebrities and movies with a currency called the Hollywood Dollar®. Traders can Buy and Sell, or Short Sell and Cover any security. HSX syndicates the data collected from the Exchange as market research to entertainment, consumer product and financial institutions and as original content to radio, television and print media. Founded in 1996, HSX is now headquartered in Los Angeles, California.

MovieStocks® represent films (both in the process of being made and that are currently in theaters). The price of a MovieStock reflects how much money people think the film will make, with each $1 million earned in US theaters equal to $1 Hollywood Dollar®. For example, if a MovieStock is priced at H$10, it means that the film is expected to make $10 million in its first four weeks in wide release. MovieStocks will be cashed out and delisted from the Exchange four weekends (typically 24 days) after they have been in wide release. The price of the MovieStock will be adjusted to reflect its exact earnings at the time it delists.

The following ERD has been provided as documentation:

docs.title: (1) SQL Q1
docs.text:
Q:

Total box office earnings to date, for each movie that had new earnings last week. You will also need a subquery here - find which movies that had earnings last week (use dynamic date filtering). Your outer query can then aggregate the total earnings for each of the movies identified by your subquery.

A:

Version 1 - Sunday as the start of the week:

WITH
Earnings_Last_Week AS (
    SELECT 
        Release_Id,
        SUM(Gross_Earnings) AS Total_Earnings_Last_Week
    FROM Box_Office_Earnings
    WHERE Earnings_Date <  DATETRUNC(WEEK, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)
    AND   Earnings_Date >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, DATETRUNC(WEEK, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP))
    GROUP BY Release_Id
    HAVING SUM(Gross_Earnings) > 0
)
SELECT
    BOR.Release_Id,
    BOR.Name AS Movie_Name,
    SUM(BOE.Gross_Earnings) AS Total_Earnings_To_Date
FROM Box_Office_Earnings AS BOE
JOIN Box_Office_Releases AS BOR ON BOE.Release_Id = BOR.Release_Id
WHERE BOE.Release_Id IN (SELECT Release_Id FROM Earnings_Last_Week)
GROUP BY BOR.Release_Id, BOR.Name
ORDER BY Total_Earnings_To_Date DESC
;

Version 2 - Monday as the start of the week:

WITH
Week_Start AS (
    SELECT DISTINCT
        Earnings_Date,
        CASE 
            -- 周一到周六：一周起点为本周一
            WHEN DATEPART(WEEKDAY, Earnings_Date) != 1 THEN DATEADD(DAY,  1, DATETRUNC(WEEK, Earnings_Date))
            -- 周日：一周起点为上周一
            ELSE                                            DATEADD(DAY, -6, DATETRUNC(WEEK, Earnings_Date))
        END AS Week_Start_Date,
        CASE 
            -- 周一到周六：一周起点为本周一
            WHEN DATEPART(WEEKDAY, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) != 1 THEN DATEADD(DAY,  1, DATETRUNC(WEEK, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP))
            -- 周日：一周起点为上周一
            ELSE                                                DATEADD(DAY, -6, DATETRUNC(WEEK, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP))
        END AS This_Week_Start_Date,
        CASE 
            -- 周一到周六：一周起点为本周一
            WHEN DATEPART(WEEKDAY, DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)) != 1 THEN DATEADD(DAY,  1, DATETRUNC(WEEK, DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)))
            -- 周日：一周起点为上周一
            ELSE                                                                  DATEADD(DAY, -6, DATETRUNC(WEEK, DATEADD(DAY, -7, CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)))
        END AS Last_Week_Start_Date
    FROM Box_Office_Earnings
),
Week_Start_Filtered AS (
    SELECT 
        Earnings_Date,
        Week_Start_Date,
        This_Week_Start_Date,
        Last_Week_Start_Date
    FROM Week_Start
    WHERE Week_Start_Date = Last_Week_Start_Date
),
Earnings_Last_Week AS (
    SELECT 
        BOE.Release_Id,
        SUM(Gross_Earnings) AS Total_Earnings_Last_Week
    FROM Box_Office_Earnings AS BOE
    JOIN Week_Start_Filtered AS WSF ON BOE.Earnings_Date = WSF.Earnings_Date
    GROUP BY BOE.Release_Id
    HAVING SUM(Gross_Earnings) > 0
)
SELECT
    BOR.Release_Id,
    BOR.Name AS Movie_Name,
    SUM(BOE.Gross_Earnings) AS Total_Earnings_To_Date
FROM Box_Office_Earnings AS BOE
JOIN Box_Office_Releases AS BOR ON BOE.Release_Id = BOR.Release_Id
WHERE BOE.Release_Id IN (SELECT Release_Id FROM Earnings_Last_Week)
GROUP BY BOR.Release_Id, BOR.Name
ORDER BY Total_Earnings_To_Date DESC
;

Q: Current price for each securities that can still actively be traded - show highest priced securities first. You will need a subqueries or two here - remember it's easier to use CTEs to develop, test, and layer subqueries. Build and test your logic piece by piece, step by step.

WITH
Security_Latest_Date AS (
    SELECT 
        Security_Symbol, 
        MAX(Price_Date) AS Latest_Price_Date
    FROM Security_Prices
    WHERE Security_Symbol IN (SELECT Security_Symbol FROM Securities WHERE Status = 'Active')

)
SELECT

    SP.Closing_Price
FROM Security_Prices      AS SP
JOIN Securities           AS S   ON SP.Security_Symbol = S.Security_Symbol
JOIN Security_Latest_Date AS SLD ON SP.Security_Symbol = SLD.Security_Symbol AND SP.Price_Date = SLD.Latest_Price_Date

docs.title: (3) SQL Q3
docs.text:
Q: For each trader and each security, the number of securities currently held, and the date and time of the last trade made. Use conditional aggregation to make this easier. Make sure you investigate the way the data is recorded, rather than making a (wrong) assumption. Note that in the stock trading world, Buy and Short open or extend holdings, whereas Sell, Cover and Delist close out holdings.

A:

WITH
Trade_Summary AS (
    SELECT
        User_Name,
        Security_Symbol,
        CASE 
            WHEN Action IN ('Buy', 'Short')            THEN Quantity
            WHEN Action IN ('Sell', 'Cover', 'Delist') THEN Quantity * -1
            ELSE 0
        END AS Quantity_Signed,
        Trade_Date_Time
    FROM Trades
)
SELECT
    T.User_Name,
    A.Trader_Name,
    T.Security_Symbol,
    S.Name AS Security_Name,
    S.Type AS Security_Type,
    SUM(T.Quantity_Signed) AS Currently_Held,
    MAX(T.Trade_Date_Time) AS Last_Trade_Date_Time
FROM Trade_Summary AS T
JOIN Accounts AS A ON T.User_Name = A.User_Name
JOIN Securities AS S ON T.Security_Symbol = S.Security_Symbol
GROUP BY T.User_Name, A.Trader_Name, T.Security_Symbol, S.Name, S.Type
HAVING SUM(T.Quantity_Signed) > 0
ORDER BY A.Trader_Name, Last_Trade_Date_Time DESC
;

docs.title: Q1
docs.text:
For how long has Global Bikes been in business?

SELECT 
    MIN(date) AS first_sales_order,
    MAX(date) AS last_sales_order
FROM sales_orders
;

========================================

first_sales_order    last_sales_order   
-------------------  -------------------
2007-01-01 00:00:00  2016-12-31 00:00:00
(1 row affected)

A date range is a perfectly valid, useful "answer" to this question. It is actually much more informative than say, "9"; 9 what?

When we see the time range, we also realise that the whole of 2007 and 2016 are included, so 10 (years) would be the more accurate answer anyway. Not subtracting the dates, or years, avoids having to think about that possibility or making the mistake without realising it in the first place. So this result is better on both counts.

docs.title: Q8
docs.text:
What is Global Bikes' discounting policy? Per product (diff. disc. for each sales order line item), or per order (same discount applied to all sales order line items)?

WITH 
order_discount AS (
    SELECT
        ordernumber,
        MIN(discount / revenue) AS min_discount_pct_temp,
        MAX(discount / revenue) AS max_discount_pct_temp,
        MAX(discount / revenue) - MIN(discount / revenue) AS diff_discount_pct_temp
    FROM sales_orders
    GROUP BY ordernumber
    HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
)
SELECT TOP 15
    ordernumber,
    ROUND(min_discount_pct_temp, 4)  AS min_discount_pct,
    ROUND(max_discount_pct_temp, 4)  AS max_discount_pct,
    ROUND(diff_discount_pct_temp, 4) AS diff_discount_pct
FROM order_discount
ORDER BY diff_discount_pct_temp DESC
;

docs.title: Tutorial 2.1 - Evaluating Data Visualization 1
docs.text:
Consider the following plot in a periodic report.

Evaluate its strengths and weaknesses, and provide recommendations for improvement.

Evaluation Checklist:

Strength:

  • The use of bar chart is correct for comparing across sparse time-interval - 12 months.
  • The plot presents raw data, without over-computation or over-precision.
  • The data is reasonably sorted by time.
  • The bars are vertically arranged without stacked bars, which is suitable for time comparison.

Weakness:

  • The plot is vague and unclear, making it difficult to identify the subject of analysis; so, it fails to provides enough information for analytical purpose.
  • The plot does not provide any takeaway or conclusive information; it merely displays the data.
  • The overall format is unclear due to excessive decoration with flashy and meaningless colors, and the use of color is redundant with the bar positions.
  • The title is not left-aligned and is too general, failing to specify what stage or type of sales, and it is not takeaway style.
  • The labels overlap with the bars making them unclear, and labeling every data point is unnecessary because it duplicates the axis. Also, the labels are overly precise.
  • The Y-axis does not indicate the unit and does not start at zero, and the scale is unreasonable with too many zeros.
  • The months are shown in a legend rather than labeled directly on the X-axis, which is hard to read.
  • The data of July is missing without any explanation.

Recommendation:

  • The chart should be redesigned to make its analytical purpose clear, and it should communicate a takeaway message that directly answers the intended question, rather than vaguely displaying numbers.
  • First, the title should be left-aligned and specific to indicate the type and period of sales, and it should be in a takeaway style to indicate key findings, for example “Sales revenue peaked in September but remained volatile throughout the year”.
  • Second, the overall design should remain clean, clear, and non-redundant. The meaningless colors should be removed. Also, the labels should be simplified, with only key points such as maximum, minimum, or targets, and overlapping labels should be avoided. Furthermore, the axis should clearly state the unit, adopt a clear scale (e.g., 1.0M instead of 1000000), and start from zero. Also, the months should be labeled directly on the X-axis instead of being shown in a legend.
  • Finally, the missing data of July, should be explained.

docs.title: Tutorial 2.2 - Evaluating Data Visualization 2
docs.text:
Consider the following plot in a periodic report.

Evaluate its strengths and weaknesses, and provide recommendations for improvement.

Evaluation Checklist:

Strength:

  • The overall format is clear without over decoration or over formatting.
  • The texts are clear without over decoration.

Weakness:

  • Using proportion-based horizontal stacked bar charts is incorrect, because they make it difficult for audience to accurately compare bar sizes and to understand the key take-away information, even though the chart title and text explain the analytical objects; so, it fails to provides enough information for analytical purpose.
  • The title simply restates the survey question rather than presenting a takeaway message, and it is centered rather than left-aligned.
  • Due to the use of proportion-based stacked bar chart, the design relies on labels to show percentages, which makes the labels overly excessive.
  • Due to the use of a proportion-based stacked bar chart, the design relies on color and legend to distinguish the categories.

Recommendation:

  • The chart should be redesigned to make its analytical purpose clear, and it should communicate a takeaway message that directly answers the intended question, rather than vaguely displaying numbers.
  • First, the chart type should be changed. The chart should display the raw counts rather than proportions, and it should use independent bars instead of stacked bars. Consequently, a single unified Y-axis can show the numbers, without relying on labeling every data point. Since the category names are long, labeling them on the X-axis would be messy, so colors and legend may still be necessary in this case.
  • Second, the title should be left-aligned and in a takeaway style to indicate key findings, for example: “Data-driven organizations are more likely to outperform financially.”.
  • Finally, the survey information can be comprehensively explained in a subtitle or annotation.

docs.title: Tutorial 2.3 - Evaluating Data Visualization 3
docs.text:
Consider the following periodic report.

Evaluate its strengths and weaknesses, and provide recommendations for improvement.

Evaluation Checklist:

Strength:

  • The overall format and texts is clear without over decoration or over formatting, and the space allocation is utilized.
  • The plots have a consistent analytical scope and periods.
  • The use of color is consistent across multiple charts.
  • The data in the plot are not overly precise.

Weakness:

  • Using pie charts is incorrect, because they make it difficult for audience to accurately compare pie sizes either within single chart or across multiple charts and to understand the key take-away information, even though the chart title and text explain the analytical objects; so, it fails to provides enough information for analytical purpose.
  • Due to the use of pie chart, the design relies on labels to show percentages and actual values, which makes the labels overly excessive.
  • Due to the use of a proportion-based stacked bar chart, the design relies on color and legend to distinguish the categories.
  • The title provides just analytical object and period without enough takeaway information.
  • The ordering of data is unreasonable: 2018/19 on left and 2017/18 on right.
  • The explanation texts are duplicated with the data presented in the plots without key conclusions.

Recommendation:

  • The chart should be redesigned to make its analytical purpose clear, and it should communicate a takeaway message that directly answers the intended question, rather than vaguely displaying numbers.
  • First, the chart type should be changed. The chart should display the raw counts only without proportions, and independent bars charts are suitable in this case, with each cluster representing a capital element and having two bars to show 2017/18 on the left and 2018/19 on the right. Consequently, for each bar chart, a single unified Y-axis can show the numbers, without relying on labeling every data point. Also, the colors and legend can be removed in this case.
  • Second, the title should be in a takeaway style to indicate key findings, for example: “Capital Renewals Dropped by £155m from 2017/18 to 2018/19.”
  • Finally, the KPIs should be should in plot titles or subtitles only, which is not necessary repeated in the paragraph.

docs.title: Tutorial 2.4 - Evaluating Data Visualization 4
docs.text:
Consider the following interactive dashboard.

Evaluate its strengths and weaknesses, and provide recommendations for improvement.

Evaluation Checklist:

Strength:

  • The overall format is clear without over decoration or over formatting: no 3D charts, no icons, and minimal borders and gridlines.
  • The layout follows a top-left to bottom-right order, with KPIs at top and detailed plots below.
  • The texts are clear. The titles, data labels, and axis labels follow a clear hierarchy and all text is horizontal, sufficiently large, and easy to read.
  • The use of axes to indicate the data rather than labels can avoid excessive labeling in the plots.
  • The colors are with semantic meaning (red = bad, blue = good), and are color-blind appropriate.

Weakness:

  • The use of map is inappropriate, which have very low data-to-ink ratio. It only uses color to display one measure with little information, and fails to answer basic questions, e.g., the top 3 profitable states.
  • The use of stacked line charts is inappropriate, because the stacked area is difficult to interpret. Also, displaying a very long period (4 years) monthly data in line charts may be meaningless, because the missing data causes distorted shapes.
  • The scale of axes are labeled with too many zeros, and not consistent across 6 line charts.
  • The color used in the map and line charts are not consistent, and the color bands in the map (50% / 3 = 16.7%) is not intuitive.
  • The KPIs are overly precise.
  • There are many filters, and some of them are unnecessary, e.g., region dropdown and profit sliders, which would make audience focus on details and ignore the overall patterns. Also, the date filters is not necessary, because users must manually adjust filters to get YTD values, which is inconvenient.

Recommendation:

  • The dashboard should be re-designed, focusing on two main measures: sales revenue and profit margin, displayed consistently across geography, customer, product, and time.
  • First, for the KPIs should have reduced numeric precision, e.g., Sales: $2.09m.
  • Second, the map showing regional sales and profit margins should be replaced with a ranked horizontal bar chart, with axis showing sales and color showing profit margin. The other two dimensions: regions and segments, should also be shown in two separate ranked bar charts, rather than using filters. The color band should be adjusted intuitively and consistently.
  • Thirdly, the time series of sales should be separately shown in a bar chart, with a fixed time range e.g., current year, last 2 years, rolling 18 months. We use bar chart here rather than line chart because we can use bar color to indicate profit margin. If using time filter, we can remove the date range filter, and apply a consistent global YTD filter.
  • Finally, we can deliver some additional insights if there is spare space, e.g., discount trends or year-on-year comparisons.

# Convert list to array
c = np.array(costs)

# Initialise empty list of product costs
product_costs = []

# For every recipe in the list of lists
for i in range(len(recipes)):

    recipe = recipes[i]
    name   = names[i]

    # Convert list to array
    r = np.array(recipe)
    
    # Multiply each element of the two arrays, then sum, to calculate the variable cost to produce product
    cost = (c * r).sum()

    # Add this product's cost to list of costs

docs.text:
The table below lists the percentage by weight of each ingredient of the total content weight for the product. For example, 1kg Nut Muesli would contain 0.2 kg of Nuts, whereas 500g Nut Muesli would contain 0.1 kg of Nuts.

Flavour Nuts (R01) Blueberries (R02) Strawberries (R03) Raisins (R04) Wheat (R05) Oats (R06) Nut 20% 30% 50% Blueberry 20% 30% 50% Strawberry 20% 30% 50% Raisin 20% 30% 50% Original 40% 60% Mixed 12% 6% 6% 6% 20% 50%

The costs of each ingredient (per kg) are listed in the table below.

Ingredient Cost per kg R01 $2.00 R02 $5.00 R03 $5.00 R04 $1.20 R05 $0.95 R06 $0.85

Note that 1 kg products also use one large box (P01) and bag (P02), and 500 g products also use one small box (P03) and bag (P04). The costs for these packaging materials are listed in the table below.

Product Size Cost Large Box 1 kg $0.30 Large Bag 1 kg $0.13 Small Box 500 g $0.23 Small Bag 500 g $0.10

To calculate the total cost of a product, we show two coding methods.

docs.title: Muesli Product Costing Using Historical Costs¶
Tutorial 3.2 - Python - Muesli Costing Using Historical Costs
docs.text:
Previously, we calculated the cost of each Muesli product using unit costs that were typed in by hand. In practice, Muesli Pty Ltd's raw material costs change over time as new purchase orders come in, so hard-coding a single cost per ingredient means the calculation quickly goes out of date.

In this tutorial we connect to the Muesli's SQL database and calculate a weighted average purchase cost for each raw material, based on actual purchase order history over a chosen time window. We then use these calculated costs — instead of manual input — to cost each product, and save the results to a CSV file so they can be reused elsewhere (e.g. combined with sales data in Tableau to analyse profitability).

Given a cutoff_date and history_weeks, the SQL to calculate the weighted average cost is:

WITH 
data_cost AS (
    SELECT
        Material_Code,
        SUM(Price * Receive_Quantity) AS Total_Cost,
        SUM(Receive_Quantity) AS Total_Quantity,
        MIN(Delivery_Date) AS First_Delivery,
        MAX(Delivery_Date) AS Last_Delivery
    FROM Purchase_Order_Items AS POI
    JOIN Purchase_Orders AS PO ON PO.Document_Number = POI.Document_Number
    WHERE PO.Delivery_Date <= '{cutoff_date}'
    AND DATEDIFF(WEEK, PO.Delivery_Date, '{cutoff_date}') < {history_weeks}
    GROUP BY Material_Code
)
SELECT
    C.Material_Code, 
    M.Material_Name,
    C.First_Delivery, 
    C.Last_Delivery,
    C.Total_Cost, 
    C.Total_Quantity,
    C.Total_Cost / C.Total_Quantity as W_Avg_Cost
FROM data_cost AS C
JOIN Materials AS M ON M.Material_Code = C.Material_Code

cutoff_date is the last day of the analysis window, and history_weeks is how many weeks prior (inclusive) to look back over.

docs.title: Program Setup
docs.text:
First, we import the necessary libraries and set up the program parameters.

import platform
import sqlalchemy as sal
import pandas as pd

cutoff_date = '2026-08-25'
history_weeks = 8

Then, we define the database connection function.

def db_connect(_driver=None):
    template = 'mssql+pyodbc:///?odbc_connect=Driver={};Server=dlyle.database.windows.net;Database=DWV;Uid=muesli;Pwd=Viz(Data);'

    if not _driver is None:
        driver = _driver
    else:
        print('Guessing driver based on', platform.system(), platform.release(), platform.machine(), platform.platform())
        if platform.system() == 'Darwin':  # MacOS
            if platform.machine() == 'arm64':  # M1 chip
                driver = '/opt/homebrew/lib/libmsodbcsql.18.dylib'
            else:
                driver = '/Library/simba/sqlserverodbc/lib/libsqlserverodbc_sbu.dylib'
        else:  # Windows and anything else
            driver = '{SQL Server}'

    c_str = template.format(driver)
    print(c_str)
    print('Attempting connection')
    cxn = sal.create_engine(c_str).connect()
    print('Success!\n')
    return cxn

Then, we retrieve the costing data from the database using the SQL query defined earlier.

sql = f"""--sql
WITH 
data_cost AS (
    SELECT
        Material_Code,
        SUM(Price * Receive_Quantity) AS Total_Cost,
        SUM(Receive_Quantity) AS Total_Quantity,
        MIN(Delivery_Date) AS First_Delivery,
        MAX(Delivery_Date) AS Last_Delivery
    FROM Purchase_Order_Items AS POI
    JOIN Purchase_Orders AS PO ON PO.Document_Number = POI.Document_Number
    WHERE PO.Delivery_Date <= '{cutoff_date}'
    AND DATEDIFF(WEEK, PO.Delivery_Date, '{cutoff_date}') < {history_weeks}
    GROUP BY Material_Code
)
SELECT
    C.Material_Code, 
    M.Material_Name,
    C.First_Delivery, 
    C.Last_Delivery,
    C.Total_Cost, 
    C.Total_Quantity,
    C.Total_Cost / C.Total_Quantity as W_Avg_Cost
FROM data_cost AS C
JOIN Materials AS M ON M.Material_Code = C.Material_Code
"""

cxn = db_connect()
dfMatCosts = pd.read_sql(sql, cxn, parse_dates=['First_Delivery', 'Last_Delivery'])
cxn.close()

Then, we calculate the cost and weight of each product based on its recipe and the unit costs of its components.

# Template for full material code including prefix
code = 'BB-{}'

# Look up unit costs by Material_Code (dfMatCosts itself is indexed positionally, for Method 1)
costs_by_code = dfMatCosts.set_index('Material_Code')['W_Avg_Cost']

# Initialise empty DataFrame of product costs
product_costs = pd.DataFrame()

# For each product recipe
for product, recipe in recipes_dict.items():
    # Re-initialise cost and weight of recipe for each product
    cost = 0
    weight = 0

    # For every component in the recipe
    for component, quantity in recipe.items():
        # Lookup cost by code, multiply by quantity used
        cost += costs_by_code.loc[code.format(component)] * quantity
        if component[0] == 'R':  # First character in string is 'R', therefore edible
            weight += quantity

    # Calculate and store this product's cost and weight
    product_costs.loc[code.format(product), 'Weight'] = weight
    product_costs.loc[code.format(product), 'Cost'] = cost

# Document the date this cost is valid to, i.e. the most recent delivery in the data

docs.title: Tutorial 3.3 - Python - Muesli Production Efficiency
docs.text:
Muesli Pty Ltd would like to better understand how efficiently the production line is operating.

Efficiency is measured by the total production output (yield) achieved, divided by the theoretical maximum capacity of the production line for the same time period.

The company has made some investments in equipment, factory layout and procedures over the past year; which have increased the theoretical daily maximum capacity:

Date Capacity 2026-01-01 24700 2026-02-26 24900 2026-03-23 25200 2026-04-21 25500 2026-05-18 25900 2026-06-16 26200 2026-07-13 26600 2026-08-10 26800

In practice, 100% efficiency is never achieved due to downtime from planned cleaning and staging that must take place every time the production line switches from producing one product to another. Maintenance and repairs, breakdowns or accidents, and supplier delays when delivering materials can also affect production.

You've been asked to write a Python program that produces a data file containing weekly historical yields vs capacity, to support analysis of production efficiency.

docs.title: Tutorial 3.4 - Python - Simulating Snakes and Ladders
docs.text:
The "Snakes and Ladders" game is a classic board game where players move their pieces according to the roll of a die, navigating a board filled with snakes and ladders that either hinder or help their progress:

  • If a player lands on a ladder base, they move up to a higher position on the board.
  • If a player lands on a snake head, they slide down to a lower position on the board.

The board is shown as follows:

When the player reaches or goes beyond the final square on the board, they win the game. In a multiple player game, the first player to reach the final square wins.

Write Python code to simulate playing 'Snakes and Ladders' for different numbers of players. Based on the range and distribution of simulated outcomes, estimate:

  • The probability that a single player completes a game in less than 40 turns.
  • The probability that 2 players complete a game in less than 30 turns.
  • The probability that 4 players complete a game in more than 15 turns.
  • With 90% confidence, what is the number of turns needed to guarantee completing a 4 player game?

simulations = 10000

docs.title: Function Definitions
docs.text:
def roll_die():
    return rnd.randint(1, 6)

def play_game(players):
    # All players start at position 0
    player_positions = [0] * players
    turns = 0

    while True:
        turns += 1
        won = False
        for p in range(players):
            pos = player_positions[p] + roll_die()

            # Ladders
            if pos == 6:
                pos = 14
            elif pos == 17:
                pos = 23
            elif pos == 27:
                pos = 33
            elif pos == 38:
                pos = 43

            # Snakes
            elif pos == 16:
                pos = 4
            elif pos == 29:
                pos = 10
            elif pos == 39:
                pos = 20
            elif pos == 45:
                pos = 34

            player_positions[p] = pos

            # This player reached the end: the game is over immediately
            if pos >= 50:
                won = True
                break

        if won:
            break

    return turns

def simulate(players):
    return [play_game(players) for _ in range(simulations)]
